keys: Compensating for Backlash in Rack-and-Pinion Drives Using Gain-Scheduled Cascade Control
history.scope: 1141 Git-tracked evidence paths, 301 members inside tar.gz, gzip contents and early baseline-index. Case/punctuation/accents normalized. Paper titles used for replication releases.

methods: Parsed the three figure CSVs and inspected all three author MATLAB scripts. Built a 0–2 m transmission envelope from TE_plus and TE_minus; linearly interpolated the full spatial grid onto measured slide positions. Compared measured x_M−x_S with both raw and plotted ±10 µm inward-shifted curves.

Used the figure 5 legend to pair indices (1,2), (3,4), (5,6), (7,8) by compensation on/off. Aligned identical timestamps on each common prefix and restricted paired moving RMS to samples whose commanded speed magnitude exceeded 1 mm/s in both runs. Entire common-prefix errors and reference mismatches are also tabulated.
results: 200,001 spatial points sampled 0–2 m give raw envelope width 20.071–73.414 µm, median 46.205 µm. Eleven time series have 136,801 total samples at 2 kHz.

All four matching moving-window RMS slide errors are lower with gain scheduling, in pair order 31.660/33.443, 31.337/33.407, 35.359/39.431, and 36.637/39.415 µm. Moving peak errors likewise decrease in all four. Two pairs have identical references; the other two differ by at most 0.097657 µm on their common time grid.
limitations: The map measures mechanical motor-to-slide transmission error. Plot boundaries and time spent outside them are neither drive-current limits nor proof of saturation. The release supplies position and K_v rather than raw torque/current or an interlock. Four pairwise comparisons on one rig are not a generalized effect estimate.
